blocks.content: An index is the single most direct lever a database gives you for making a slow query fast, and yet indexing well is one of the most commonly misunderstood parts of working with a database. This topic is about the practical side, when to add an index, which columns to index and in what order, and what it actually costs you in return. The internal mechanics of how an index is actually implemented on disk are covered separately under B-Trees and B+ Trees elsewhere in this course.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522581-923726.png
blocks.alt: Without an index, finding a row means checking every single one; with the right index, the database jumps straight to it

blocks.content: 1. What Indexing Actually Does for a Read
blocks.text: 1. What Indexing Actually Does for a Read

blocks.content: Without an index, finding rows matching a condition means a full table scan, checking every single row, one at a time, to see if it matches. For a table with a few hundred rows, that is instant. For a table with a hundred million rows, that same scan can take seconds, an eternity for anything a user is actively waiting on.

An index maintains a separate, sorted structure, almost always a B+ Tree, mapping column values directly to the rows that hold them. With that structure in place, finding matching rows becomes a fast, targeted lookup instead of an exhaustive scan.

It helps to picture an index the way you would the index at the back of a textbook, finding every mention of a specific term without an index means reading the entire book page by page. The index at the back lets you jump directly to the relevant pages instead, at the cost of the book being a little longer and needing that index to be updated whenever content changes.

It is worth being precise that an index does not eliminate the underlying cost of finding data, it changes the shape of that cost entirely, from a cost that grows with the size of the whole table, to a cost that grows with the depth of the index structure instead, a much smaller and slower-growing number.
1.1 Why this scales so poorly without an index
blocks.text: 1.1 Why this scales so poorly without an index

blocks.content: The cost of a full table scan grows linearly with the size of the table, twice the rows means roughly twice the scan time. An indexed lookup, by contrast, grows logarithmically, doubling the table size adds only a small, roughly constant amount of extra work, exactly the same shallow-tree benefit covered under B-Trees and B+ Trees elsewhere in this course.

This gap only widens as data grows, which is exactly why a missing index rarely shows up as a problem in a small development database with a few thousand test rows, and only becomes visible once real production data volume, millions or billions of rows, actually arrives, a common and painful surprise for teams that never load-tested against realistic data sizes.
2. The Cost Side Nobody Skips: Slower Writes
blocks.text: 2. The Cost Side Nobody Skips: Slower Writes

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522582-42493660.png
blocks.alt: Every write to an indexed column has to update not just the table, but every single index built on that table too

blocks.content: An index is not free. Every single insert, update, or delete that touches an indexed column has to update that index too, in addition to the actual table data. A table with five indexes pays that update cost five separate times on every relevant write, not once. This is the trade-off that makes indexing a decision, not a default, more indexes always means faster reads on those specific columns and slower writes across the board.

This cost is not hypothetical, it compounds directly with the number of indexes on a table. A table with ten indexes pays ten separate index update operations for every single insert, which is exactly why write-heavy tables tend to be indexed far more conservatively than read-heavy ones.

It is worth remembering this cost is not only about raw write latency either, every index also consumes real disk space and memory, a table with many large indexes can end up spending more total storage on its indexes than on the actual data they are indexing.

It is worth stating this trade-off plainly to anyone reviewing a schema change, adding an index in response to a slow read is a legitimate, common fix, but it should be a deliberate decision weighed against its write cost, not an automatic reflex applied to every column that appears in any query at all.
3. Choosing Which Columns to Index
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522582-743698323.png
blocks.alt: A column with only two possible values barely narrows anything down; a column that is nearly unique per row narrows a search dramatically

blocks.content: The concept that matters most here is selectivity, how much an index on a given column actually narrows down a search. An index on a boolean "is_active" flag with only two possible values does little to help, since roughly half the table still matches either value. An index on an email address, nearly unique per row, narrows a million-row table down to essentially one match immediately.

["Columns used in WHERE clauses, especially with high selectivity, are strong candidates.","Columns used in JOIN conditions almost always deserve an index, since joins are exactly where an unindexed lookup gets expensive fast.","Columns used in ORDER BY benefit too, since a sorted index can satisfy the ordering without a separate, expensive sort step."]
items: Columns used in WHERE clauses, especially with high selectivity, are strong candidates.
Columns used in JOIN conditions almost always deserve an index, since joins are exactly where an unindexed lookup gets expensive fast.
Columns used in ORDER BY benefit too, since a sorted index can satisfy the ordering without a separate, expensive sort step.

blocks.content: Foreign key columns deserve special mention here, many databases do not automatically index a foreign key column just because it references another table, leaving joins on that relationship slow by default until an index is added deliberately, a detail easy to miss when a schema is first designed.

It is also worth checking whether a unique constraint already implies an index before adding a redundant one, most databases automatically create an index to enforce a unique or primary key constraint, and adding a second, separate index on that same column is pure, unnecessary overhead.
3.1 A quick selectivity gut check

A useful rough test: if a value in the column would only match a tiny fraction of the table rows, it is likely a good indexing candidate. If a value matches a large fraction of the table, closer to being the majority case, an index is far less likely to actually help.

A concrete number helps here too, a column where each value matches roughly 1 percent of rows or fewer is generally an excellent indexing candidate, while a column where a single value matches 30 percent or more of the table often gains little from an index at all.
4. Composite Indexes and Column Order
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283899104-76382595.png
blocks.alt: A composite index on (a, b, c) can serve queries on a alone, or a and b together, but not on b alone

blocks.content: A composite index spans multiple columns at once, and column order within it matters enormously. An index on (country, city, zip_code) can efficiently serve a query filtering on country alone, or country and city together, or all three, because those all match a left-to-right prefix of the index. It cannot efficiently serve a query filtering on zip_code alone, since that is not a prefix of the index at all.

blocks.title: A practical rule of thumb
blocks.content: Order the columns in a composite index from most selective and most commonly filtered alone, down to least selective, so the widest range of queries can still benefit from at least a useful prefix of the index.

It is also worth resisting the temptation to build a separate single-column index for every column already covered by a composite index, in most cases the composite index already serves those simpler queries too, and the extra single-column index just adds redundant write overhead.

This left-to-right prefix rule is easy to forget under pressure, and a surprisingly common source of a query mysteriously not benefiting from an index that clearly exists, worth double checking directly against the actual WHERE clause whenever a composite index does not seem to be helping as expected.

Designing a good composite index usually starts from the actual queries a table needs to serve, listing out the most frequent and most performance-sensitive queries first, then working backward to a column order that serves as many of them as possible, rather than guessing at a sensible order in isolation.
5. Covering Indexes: Avoiding the Extra Lookup
blocks.text: 5. Covering Indexes: Avoiding the Extra Lookup

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522583-410477980.png
blocks.alt: A covering index already contains every column a query needs, skipping the extra trip back to the full table row

blocks.content: Normally, once an index finds a matching row, the database still has to do a second lookup back into the actual table to fetch any columns the query needs that are not part of the index itself. A covering index includes every column the query actually needs, letting the database answer the entire query from the index alone, without that second lookup.

The trade-off here is real too, a covering index has to store more columns, making it physically larger and costing more to maintain on every write, precisely the same read-versus-write tension that runs through this entire topic, just applied one level deeper.
5.1 A concrete example

Consider a query selecting only a user id and display name where the id matches a specific value. An ordinary index on id still requires fetching the display name from the full table row. An index that includes both id and display_name together can answer the entire query directly from the index, never touching the underlying table at all, a meaningful savings on a hot, frequently run query.

This same idea extends naturally to any frequently run, narrow query, identifying the small handful of columns a hot query actually needs and building a covering index around exactly those tends to yield some of the largest, most targeted performance wins available without changing any application code at all.
6. When an Index Gets Ignored by the Query Planner
blocks.text: 6. When an Index Gets Ignored by the Query Planner

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283903013-702256030.png
blocks.alt: Even with an index available, the planner can decide a full scan is actually cheaper, especially on a low-cardinality column

blocks.content: Having an index does not guarantee the database will actually use it. The query planner estimates the cost of every available approach and picks the cheapest one, and for a low-selectivity column, or a small table, scanning the whole table can genuinely be cheaper than the overhead of using an index at all. This is not a bug, it is the planner doing its job correctly, and it is exactly why simply adding an index is not always enough to make a slow query fast, covered further under Query Optimization elsewhere in this section.

["Check the actual execution plan rather than assuming an index is being used just because it exists.","Consider whether the table is simply small enough that a full scan genuinely is the faster choice.","Verify the query is actually written in a way the planner can match against the index at all, covered further under Query Optimization."]
items: Check the actual execution plan rather than assuming an index is being used just because it exists.
Consider whether the table is simply small enough that a full scan genuinely is the faster choice.
Verify the query is actually written in a way the planner can match against the index at all, covered further under Query Optimization.

blocks.content: Query planners also periodically rely on collected statistics about how data is actually distributed in a table, if those statistics go stale after a large data change, the planner can make a poor choice temporarily, until those statistics are refreshed, a detail worth knowing when a previously fast query suddenly slows down for no apparent reason.

Forcing a planner to use a specific index is sometimes possible through database-specific hints, but this is generally discouraged as a first resort, since it fights against the planner own, usually more accurate, cost estimates rather than addressing whatever caused it to make a different choice in the first place.

This is precisely why measuring, rather than assuming, matters so much here, the only reliable way to know whether an index actually helps a specific query is to look at the real execution plan the database chooses, not to reason about it purely from first principles.
7. Over-Indexing: A Real, Common Mistake
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522583-795242323.png
blocks.alt: A pile of rarely-used indexes means every single write pays a real, ongoing cost with little corresponding benefit

blocks.content: It is tempting to index defensively, adding an index for every column that might someday be queried. This is a real, common mistake, every added index is a permanent tax on every future write to that table, whether or not that index ever actually gets used by a real query. Periodically auditing and removing genuinely unused indexes is a normal, healthy part of database maintenance, not an afterthought.

Most databases expose tooling specifically to spot this, PostgreSQL index usage statistics, MySQL performance schema, or a cloud provider managed database insights, all of which can surface indexes that have gone unused for an extended period, strong candidates for removal.

This is a genuinely easy trap to fall into during active development, adding an index the moment a query feels slow, without first confirming the index is actually the bottleneck, or whether the underlying query itself needs rewriting instead, a distinction covered in full under Query Optimization.

This is a good place to apply the same cost-benefit thinking used elsewhere in system design generally, an index is worth keeping only if the read benefit it provides genuinely outweighs the write cost it imposes, not simply because it exists or was added defensively at some point in the past.
8. Real-World Usage

{"headers":["Database","Notes"],"rows":[["PostgreSQL","Supports B-Tree (default), hash, GiST, and GIN index types for different data patterns"],["MySQL (InnoDB)","Primary key is automatically a clustered B+ Tree index; secondary indexes are separate trees"],["MongoDB","Supports single-field, compound, and covering indexes with similar trade-offs"]]}

It is worth checking the actual documentation for whichever database is in use, since index behavior, available types, and syntax vary meaningfully between systems, general principles like selectivity and composite ordering transfer everywhere, but the exact tooling to inspect and manage indexes does not.

It is a healthy habit to review index usage as part of a regular maintenance cadence, not just when a specific query is reported as slow, since the absence of a complaint does not necessarily mean the current set of indexes is actually well matched to how the table is really being queried.
8.1 Different index types for different jobs
blocks.text: 8.1 Different index types for different jobs

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522584-562052986.png
blocks.alt: A B-Tree index handles both equality and range queries; a hash index is faster for equality alone but useless for ranges

blocks.content: Not every index needs to be a B-Tree. A hash index can be faster for pure equality lookups, but offers no support at all for range queries or sorting, exactly the gap covered under B-Trees and B+ Trees elsewhere in this course. Specialized index types like PostgreSQL GIN and GiST exist specifically for full-text search, array containment, and geospatial queries, covered further in the Handling Location Data pattern.
8.2 Partial indexes
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396522584-665299646.png
blocks.alt: Indexing only the subset of rows that actually matter keeps the index smaller and cheaper to maintain

blocks.content: A partial index only indexes rows matching a specific condition, for example, only orders where status = 'pending', rather than every order ever placed. If queries only ever care about that subset, a partial index can be dramatically smaller and cheaper to maintain than a full index across the entire table.

Picking the wrong index type is a subtler mistake than picking no index at all, a hash index on a column that later needs a range query silently fails to help that new query, forcing a full scan anyway, even though an index technically exists on that column.

Partial indexing works especially well for tables mixing a large volume of historical, rarely-queried rows with a much smaller, actively-queried subset, an orders table where only pending orders are checked frequently is a textbook case for a partial index scoped to just that status.
9. Common Mistakes

["Indexing a low-selectivity column expecting a speedup that never really materializes.","Building a composite index in the wrong column order for the queries that actually run against it.","Never revisiting indexes as query patterns evolve, leaving stale, unused indexes quietly taxing every write."]
items: Indexing a low-selectivity column expecting a speedup that never really materializes.
Building a composite index in the wrong column order for the queries that actually run against it.
Never revisiting indexes as query patterns evolve, leaving stale, unused indexes quietly taxing every write.

blocks.content: A further, subtle mistake is indexing a column that gets modified extremely frequently for reasons unrelated to how it is queried, a last_updated timestamp touched on every write is a poor indexing candidate if nothing actually queries by it, since it pays the full write cost with no corresponding read benefit.

It is also a mistake to assume adding an index is always risk-free to try, on a very large, actively written table, building a new index can itself be an expensive, locking operation that needs to be scheduled and executed carefully, not something to run casually against a live production table without a plan.

It is also worth mentioning function-based indexing as a related, easy-to-miss detail, filtering on LOWER(email) needs an index built specifically on that expression, an ordinary index on the raw email column will not help a query that transforms the column before comparing it.
10. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 10. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: Strong answers lead with the read-versus-write trade-off explicitly, rather than treating indexing as an unconditional win. Being able to explain selectivity, composite index column ordering, and covering indexes shows real, practical experience beyond just knowing that "indexes make queries faster."
An index is not free speed, it is speed borrowed from every future write against that table.

A good follow-up to anticipate is being asked how you would identify which indexes an existing production table actually needs, a strong answer references looking at real, observed query patterns and execution plans rather than guessing based on the schema alone, since the queries that actually run in production are the only thing that truly matters here.

Naming the specific trade-off, faster targeted reads against slower, more expensive writes, and being able to reason through a concrete example rather than reciting a definition, is consistently what separates a memorized answer from one that demonstrates real, hands-on database experience.
Key Takeaways

["An index turns an expensive full table scan into a fast, targeted lookup, at the real cost of slower writes on every indexed column.","Selectivity, how much a column actually narrows down a search, determines whether indexing it is worthwhile at all.","Composite index column order matters, an index serves queries matching its left-to-right prefix, not any arbitrary subset of its columns.","A covering index avoids an extra lookup back to the full table by including every column a query needs directly.","The query planner can choose to ignore an available index if it estimates a full scan would actually be cheaper.","Over-indexing is a real, common mistake, every unused index is a permanent, ongoing cost on writes with no offsetting benefit."]
items: An index turns an expensive full table scan into a fast, targeted lookup, at the real cost of slower writes on every indexed column.
Selectivity, how much a column actually narrows down a search, determines whether indexing it is worthwhile at all.
Composite index column order matters, an index serves queries matching its left-to-right prefix, not any arbitrary subset of its columns.
A covering index avoids an extra lookup back to the full table by including every column a query needs directly.
The query planner can choose to ignore an available index if it estimates a full scan would actually be cheaper.
Over-indexing is a real, common mistake, every unused index is a permanent, ongoing cost on writes with no offsetting benefit.

blocks.content: Read this topic alongside Query Optimization and B-Trees and B+ Trees in this course, together they cover the full picture, why an index works internally, how to design one deliberately, and how to confirm a query is actually using it as intended.

Treat indexing as an ongoing, iterative practice rather than a one-time schema decision, real query patterns evolve as an application grows, and the right set of indexes for a table today is rarely still the right set two years later without ever revisiting it.
